_howTo: Questions for the quiz, on the ideas behind the lessons. Edit freely. "answer" is the index of the right option. Cards about each cloud's look, causes and weather, and the photo cards, are made from core/clouds.ts and the photo library, not from this file.

cards.question: What is the white plume over a boiling kettle made of?
options: Tiny droplets of liquid water
Water vapour, the gas itself
Hot air, rising off the water
cards.why: Water vapour is invisible. The plume starts a finger’s width from the spout, where the vapour has cooled and clumped into droplets that scatter light.

cards.question: What is the dew point?
options: The temperature the air must be cooled to before its vapour condenses
The temperature at which morning dew evaporates again
The temperature the air happens to be at right now
cards.why: Cool air to its dew point and the excess vapour condenses into droplets. It depends only on how much vapour there is.

cards.question: You add more water vapour to a jar of air. What happens to its dew point?
options: It goes up
It goes down
It stays the same
cards.why: More crowded vapour starts sticking with less cooling, so the dew point rises. A high dew point means humid air.

cards.question: What does a cloud droplet need to form on?
options: A speck of dust, smoke or salt
Another droplet, already formed
Nothing: vapour clumps on its own
cards.why: A cluster of a few molecules falls apart. A speck gives them a surface to gather on, and the air holds millions of them in every lungful.

cards.question: Why does a clear night get colder than a cloudy one?
options: The ground’s heat radiates straight out to space
Clear air is colder to begin with than cloudy air
Clouds give off heat of their own, warming the ground
cards.why: Under a clear sky the ground’s infrared escapes to space. A cloud sends some of it back down, like a blanket.

cards.question: What kind of night makes valley fog by dawn?
options: Clear, calm and damp
Cloudy, windy and damp
Clear, windy and dry
cards.why: A clear sky lets the ground cool, calm air leaves the chill at the bottom, and damp air has its dew point close by.

cards.question: What is an inversion?
options: Warmer air lying on top of colder air
Colder air lying on top of warmer air
Air that rises and sinks in endless loops
cards.why: Normally air gets colder going up. In an inversion it gets warmer, which is the most stable arrangement: nothing rises through it.

cards.question: What is the difference between fog and stratus?
options: Only whether the base touches the ground
Fog is made of vapour, and stratus of droplets
Stratus is much higher, up on the middle floor
cards.why: They are the same cloud. Lift a fog bank off the valley floor and it is called stratus.

cards.question: How does morning fog clear?
options: From the bottom up, as the sun warms the ground
From the top down, as the sun warms its top
All at once, as the morning wind blows it away
cards.why: The sun warms the ground, the ground warms the air touching it, and the lowest droplets evaporate first, often leaving a layer of stratus for a while.

cards.question: Why does rising air cool?
options: It expands into the lower pressure higher up
It touches colder air on the way up
It loses its water vapour as it climbs
cards.why: With less air pressing down, it spreads out, and the work of spreading out comes from its own molecules’ energy.

cards.question: How fast does a rising bubble of clear air cool?
options: About 10 °C per kilometre
About 2 °C per kilometre
About 6.5 °C per kilometre
cards.why: 10 °C per kilometre, every day. (6.5 is the average of the air around, and 2 is how fast the bubble’s dew point falls.)

cards.question: Temperature 26 °C, dew point 14 °C. Where will cumulus bases be?
options: About 1,500 metres up
About 125 metres up
About 12 kilometres up
cards.why: The gap closes by 8 °C per kilometre, so each degree is about 125 m: 12 × 125 = 1,500 m.

cards.question: On a humid day, are cumulus bases low or high?
options: Low
High
Humidity makes no difference
cards.why: Humid air starts with its dew point close to its temperature, so a rising bubble reaches it quickly.

cards.question: When is the air unstable?
options: When it cools with height faster than a rising bubble does
When it cools with height more slowly than a rising bubble does
When it is warmer and damper at the ground than it was yesterday
cards.why: Then a nudged bubble stays warmer than its neighbours and keeps rising on its own.

cards.question: Why does a cloudy bubble cool only about 5 °C per kilometre, not 10?
options: Condensing water gives off heat
The cloud shades it from the sun
It stops expanding inside the cloud
cards.why: Condensing vapour releases the heat it took to evaporate (latent heat), warming the bubble from within.

cards.question: Why do the cumulus in one sky share the same flat base?
options: The air they rise from is well mixed, so they reach their dew point at the same height
A layer of warm air above presses every heap down to the same flat level
Gravity pulls the droplets in every cloud down to one level at the bottom
cards.why: By mid-morning thermals have stirred the lowest kilometre evenly, so every bubble condenses at nearly the same height.

cards.question: What decides which floor a cloud belongs to?
options: The temperature where it forms, which sets what it is made of
Only how thick it is, from its base to its top
Whether it rains, and how hard the rain falls
cards.why: Low clouds are liquid droplets, high clouds are ice; the middle is a mix. Heights are only guides.

cards.question: A cloud has soft, feathery edges. Which floor is it most likely on?
options: High: it is made of ice
Low: it is made of droplets
Middle: it is made of both
cards.why: Ice crystals linger and trail off; crowded droplets evaporate in seconds and leave crisp edges.

cards.question: A lumpy layer’s pieces look about as wide as your thumb at arm’s length. What is it?
options: Altocumulus
Stratocumulus
Cirrocumulus
cards.why: Wider than three fingers is stratocumulus; smaller than your little-finger nail is cirrocumulus; in between is altocumulus.

cards.question: Why do most clouds never rain?
options: Their droplets are too small to fall far before evaporating
They are too high for their drops to reach the ground before melting
They are made of vapour, which has to turn to liquid before it falls
cards.why: A raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets, and only a deep cloud gives drops time to grow that big.

cards.question: Most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C are made of…
options: Liquid droplets, supercooled
Ice crystals, frozen solid
Water vapour, not yet condensed
cards.why: Droplets need a rare ice-shaped speck to freeze. Without one they stay liquid down to about −38 °C.

cards.question: Where does most summer rain start?
options: As snow high in the cloud
As droplets near the base
As hail in the updraught
cards.why: Ice crystals grow fast at the expense of supercooled droplets, fall as snow, and melt below the freezing level.

cards.question: A ring 22° around the sun means the sky is full of…
options: Hexagonal ice crystals: cirrostratus
Water droplets: altostratus
Fine dust: a dry haze
cards.why: Hexagonal crystals act as 60° prisms that bend light by at least about 22°. A thickening halo veil often means rain within a day.

cards.question: In what order do clouds arrive ahead of a warm front?
options: Cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus
Nimbostratus, altostratus, cirrostratus, cirrus
Cumulus, cumulonimbus, stratus, then clear
cards.why: Warm air slides up a gentle slope over the cold, so its highest clouds show first, up to a day and a half ahead.

cards.question: Why does a thunderstorm’s top spread into a flat anvil?
options: It hits the tropopause, where the air starts warming with height
The wind is strongest at the top, and blows the tower flat
The ice crystals are lighter than droplets, so they float out
cards.why: Above the tropopause the stratosphere warms with height, a lid that even a storm updraught can barely pierce.

cards.question: You count 9 seconds between flash and thunder. How far away was the strike?
options: About 3 km
About 9 km
About 30 km
cards.why: Sound takes about 3 seconds per kilometre. Under 30 seconds, the storm is close enough to strike you: go indoors.

cards.question: A smooth lens-shaped cloud sits still over a ridge in a strong wind. What makes it?
options: A standing wave in stable air flowing over the mountain
A thunderstorm about to form in the rising air over the mountain
Smoke from a fire, caught and held in the still air over the ridge
cards.why: Air rises over each wave crest, condenses, and evaporates again on the way down, so the cloud stays put while the wind blows through it.

cards.question: Little turrets sprout from altocumulus on a warm morning. What should you expect?
options: Thunderstorms later in the day
A clear, calm afternoon
Fog in the valley tonight
cards.why: Castellanus shows the middle sky is already unstable, so afternoon thermals can climb into storms.

cards.question: A barometer has fallen steadily, about 1 hPa every three hours, since morning. What does it say?
options: A low is on its way
A high is building
Nothing: only the number matters
cards.why: Pressure falls as a low comes, because air near its centre rises out of the column overhead faster than it flows in. The trend matters more than the number.

cards.question: What does a barometer actually measure?
options: The weight of the column of air overhead
How much water vapour is in the air
How fast the wind is blowing overhead
cards.why: About ten tonnes of air stand on every square metre, enough to hold up 760 mm of mercury. A lighter column means lower pressure.

cards.question: The warm front has just gone by. What changes?
options: The wind veers to the southwest, it turns mild and muggy, and the barometer steadies
The wind swings northwest, it turns cold and clear, and the barometer jumps
The wind backs to the east, it turns chilly and damp, and the barometer falls
cards.why: Behind the warm front is the warm sector: warm, humid air, a south or southwest wind and a nearly steady barometer, until the cold front comes.

cards.question: What does a cold front usually bring as it passes?
options: A line of towering cloud, a gusty squall and brief heavy showers, then clearing and colder air
Hours of light, steady rain from a wide, smooth sheet, then mild and muggy air
Fog and drizzle that settle in for the night, then a still, frosty morning
cards.why: Dense cold air drives in under warm air with a steep nose, lifting it fast enough to set off towers. The wind swings west or northwest and the barometer jumps.

cards.question: Why does a warm front bring long, steady rain and a cold front short, heavy showers?
options: A warm front lifts air slowly up a gentle ramp; a cold front shoves it up a steep nose
A warm front carries far more water, and a cold front only what is left
A cold front moves more slowly, so its rain has longer to build up
cards.why: Lifting speed is the front’s speed times its slope. Gentle lifting spreads the rain over a wide belt; steep lifting squeezes it into a narrow band.

cards.question: With your back to the wind (north of the equator), where is low pressure?
options: On your left, a little ahead
On your right, a little ahead
Straight behind you
cards.why: Buys Ballot’s rule, 1857. South of the equator it is on your right.

cards.question: Your back is to the surface wind, and high cirrus is moving across from your left. What does that suggest?
options: A low is approaching: the weather will get worse
The low is moving away: the weather will improve
Nothing: high cloud never says anything
cards.why: The crossed-winds rule. High cloud from your right would mean the low is moving away.

cards.question: Why does air reach the Columbia Basin drier and warmer than it left the coast?
options: It rains out on the Cascades’ western slopes, then warms at the dry rate all the way down
The basin is lower, so the air is squeezed and warmed by the weight above it
The Columbia River warms the air as it flows across the basin from the coast
cards.why: Going up, the air cools at the dry rate, then more slowly as cloud. Coming down with no cloud left, it warms at the full dry rate: a rain shadow.

cards.question: Why can a supercooled cloud sit for hours without snowing?
options: It has almost no ice to start with: ice-starting specks are rare
It has too little water to make even one snowflake
Its droplets are too warm to freeze, even below 0 °C
cards.why: At −10 °C a litre of cloud has about a hundred thousand droplets and perhaps one ice-starting speck in every few hundred litres. What it lacks is ice, not water.

cards.question: How does dry ice make a supercooled cloud snow?
options: It chills its trail below −40 °C, where droplets and vapour freeze on their own
Its crystals are shaped like ice, so droplets freeze onto them
It adds water to the cloud, so the droplets grow heavy and fall
cards.why: Dry ice is −78 °C. It works by cold alone, in any cloud colder than 0 °C, leaving hundreds of billions of crystals per gram.

cards.question: Why does silver iodide start ice?
options: Its six-sided crystals are spaced almost exactly like ice
It is very cold, colder even than dry ice
It soaks up the water vapour around it
cards.why: Its atoms sit only 1.5 percent further apart than the molecules of ice, so droplets freeze on it as if it were ice, below about −5 °C.

cards.question: A layer was seeded with far too much dry ice. What happens?
options: So many crystals share the water that they stay too small to fall
It snows twice as hard as a layer seeded properly
Nothing: the extra dry ice just melts and falls away
cards.why: Overseeding. Tens to hundreds of crystals per litre snow a layer out; thousands per litre leave a lingering veil of ice.

cards.question: Can seeding make rain from a cloud warmer than 0 °C all through?
options: No: there is no supercooled water for ice to grow from
Yes: dry ice chills it enough to freeze
Yes: silver iodide works in any cloud
cards.why: Seeding gives ice to supercooled water. A warm cloud has nothing to freeze.

cards.question: Why can’t seeding end a drought under a strong high?
options: Sinking air keeps the sky clear: there is no cloud to seed
Seeding only works at night, and droughts are hot by day
The air is too cold under a high for the seeds to work
cards.why: Seeding cannot lift air or make cloud. It can only give ice to supercooled water that is already there.

cards.question: How can you tell whether seeding really added snow?
options: Seed storms picked by chance and compare with unseeded ones over many winters
Seed the storms that look most promising and see if they snow
Seed one big storm and measure its snow very closely
cards.why: Storms vary so much by themselves that only chance-picked storms, in large numbers, can show a real effect of ten or fifteen percent.

cards.question: The dew point is 21 °C (70 °F). How does the air feel?
options: Muggy and oppressive
Crisp and dry
Fresh and cool
cards.why: Below about 10 °C (50 °F) the air feels crisp; around 16 to 18 °C (60 to 65 °F) sticky; above 20 °C (68 °F) muggy, because sweat can barely evaporate.

cards.question: Contrails behind high aeroplanes linger, widen and spread into a sheet. What does that say?
options: The high air is moist, as it is ahead of a storm
The high air is dry, and fair weather is holding
Nothing: contrails always look like that
cards.why: A contrail is ice made by the engines. In dry high air it evaporates in seconds; in air close to full of vapour it lasts and spreads, as it does far out ahead of a storm.

cards.question: Grey streaks hang from a high cloud base and fade out halfway to the ground. What are they?
options: Virga: rain evaporating before it lands
Scud: torn shreds of low cloud
Fallstreaks: ice from an aeroplane
cards.why: Rain or snow falling into dry air evaporates on the way down. The cloud is raining, but the ground stays dry.

cards.question: On a hot, still afternoon under a dark tower, the air turns suddenly cool and gusty. What is coming?
options: The downpour and lightning, within minutes
A cold front, with a day of steady rain
Clear skies, as the storm has died
cards.why: The cool rush is the storm’s downdraught spreading along the ground: the gust front, usually 5 to 15 minutes ahead of the downpour and the lightning.

cards.question: A radar map shows a thin, ragged line of red and magenta marching in from the west. What is it?
options: A cold front’s squall line, with downpours and hail
A warm front’s wide shield of steady rain
A layer of cloud too thin to rain at all
cards.why: A cold front’s steep nose crams its rain into a narrow line of towers. Red is a downpour and magenta hail; a warm front shows as a wide, smooth shield of green.
